prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms held in a magic-wavelength lattice are interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and trap light shifts, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I have moved from B031 to B041, and I want to say plainly why. The chair asked whether my seventh place for lattice clocks was a scientific objection or an overlap objection. It was an overlap objection, and having reread the exchange I think it does not hold. Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce and Kroll point to the same distinction: the 2005 prize honoured the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions and photons in cavities, whereas the lattice clock solves a different problem, namely how to hold millions of neutral atoms tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil effects without the trap shifting the clock transition. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a quantitative atomic-structure prediction, and the 1e-18 uncertainty budgets of Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in several continents are exactly the kind of independent, reproducible test I look for. The question of what has been learned about nature has a concrete answer: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre height differences, and the first laboratory-scale bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings. No deviation from known physics has been seen, and I would not claim one; but a measurement that makes general relativity a laboratory tool at this level opens a new regime of observation. The two-name credit, Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking the platform to record accuracy and stability with many-body effects under control, is the cleanest on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterarguments remain these. Lattice clocks are close to two earlier metrology prizes, and a sceptic can read them as an outstanding instrument achievement and not as a change in our picture of nature; Danielsson's point that no deviation from known physics has appeared is correct. Two names do not reflect the contributions of PTB, SYRTE, Takamoto and the other lattice-clock groups, and Ye's role in the comb work could be read as double credit unless the citation is built around the lattice clock alone. The redefinition of the second has not been decided, so some of the practical payoff is still prospective. Finally, B032 has the stronger conceptual claim as a new organising principle, and my deference on condensed matter means I cannot weigh that case as well as Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson can.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B041 as a new measurement capability, wants the dates of early lattice-clock demonstrations and 1e-18 values checked, and asked me earlier about the overlap with the comb and ion-control prizes.
responses.response: I agree with his reading, and it changes my position. My own first-round worry was overlap with 2005 and 2012, and his answer, many-atom Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with engineered cancellation of the trap shift, is a different principle from either. As someone who works on the circuit side, I recognise the same pattern as in circuit QED: a new way of coupling a quantum system to a controlled environment that opens a regime. I also agree that the historical dates and uncertainty values quoted from memory must be checked in the expert reports before the citation is final. Where I would be careful is the redefinition of the second: I would not make the prize depend on it, since the physics and inter-laboratory agreement already exist.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the citation to say what is learned about nature, not only that precision was reached, and would hold at two names unless the record shows an earlier originator.
responses.response: I support both points. A citation built on the invention of the magic-wavelength lattice clock, with millimetre-scale redshift and bounds on constants as the demonstrated consequences, answers the instrument objection better than a bare statement of accuracy. I also agree with holding at Katori and Ye: adding a third name would dilute a credit that is clear, and the committee is not obliged to list every contributor. Her observation that clocks in Japan, the US, Germany, France and China agree on frequency ratios is the strongest maturity evidence on the table, and I weigh it above the overlap concern that led me to rank B041 seventh.

responses.point: Mehlig asked in round 1 whether circuit QED contains a physical discovery distinct from the 2025 tunnelling prize or is mostly an architecture, and ranked B031 eighth on timing and on the cut of the credit at three.
responses.response: I still think circuit QED is a distinct physical result, namely strong coupling of a single microwave photon to an engineered atom with dispersive readout, which the 2025 laureates did not do. But I accept that I could not persuade anyone else of it in round 1, that the Girvin and Huang credit is painful at three names, and that a circuit prize immediately after 2025 invites a timing objection. Together with my disclosed proximity, that is enough for me to stop arguing for it as the committee's choice. I keep it as my first alternative because I believe the physics is sound and the committee may want it in a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson notes that no deviation from known physics has yet been seen with lattice clocks and prefers B032, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, covering theory, the 2D experiment and 3D ARPES.
responses.response: His point that clocks have not yet found new physics is fair, and I will not claim otherwise; the citation should be worded around the technique and the tests it makes possible. But I would apply the same standard to B032 that I asked others to apply to B031: any trio there leaves out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang or Fu, and the committee is split by one name between Mele and Hasan. I am not able to judge priority in ARPES or the HgTe proposal, and I defer to him and Eriksson on that. The difference for me is that the two-name B041 credit does not require us to resolve such a dispute. If the committee settles on B032 I could support it, and I have listed it as an alternative.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the citation be built around the magic-wavelength lattice clock and that Ye's comb work and the early demonstration dates be handled carefully.
responses.response: I agree, and it also settles my overlap objection for me: if the citation is tied to the lattice clock and not to combs, the 2005 laureates and Ye's earlier work are not the object of the award. I would like the expert reports to confirm who first realised strontium magic-wavelength spectroscopy and who first reached 1e-18, as she suggests, and I accept that this check could strengthen the two-name case or reveal a missing name. I would reconsider the configuration only if the record shows a different originator.

uncertainties: Whether the verified chronology of the first strontium lattice clock, the first magic-wavelength spectroscopy and the first 1e-18 evaluation supports Katori and Ye alone, or points to another originator.
Whether the committee will accept lattice clocks as a discovery that opens a regime (millimetre redshift, bounds on constants and dark matter) when no deviation from known physics has been seen.
Whether B032 deserves more weight than I give it, since I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp-Hasan attribution.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing, which I think it should not.
Whether circuit QED, which I still consider a distinct and robust physical result, is better recognised in a later year given the 2025 prize.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in the Chalmers superconducting-circuit community closest to B031 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf), which I no longer prefer. I have no personal connection to those three. For B041 I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye and no institutional tie to optical lattice clock groups. Because I am no longer advocating B031, I think discounting my first-round ranking is sufficient and I do not ask for recusal, but I leave that decision to the committee. My relationship with Kroll is institutional only, through WACQT.
